title: Chablis and the Côte de Beaune
subtitle: Burgundy's white heart

steps.title: Chablis
steps.body: Chablis, in northern Burgundy, is cool and continental, with frost risk. Its Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of tiny oyster fossils, gives lean, mineral, high-acid wines with green apple, lemon and a flinty, saline edge. Most Chablis is unoaked; Grand Crus often see some oak. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and seven Grand Crus.

steps.title: The Côte de Beaune
steps.body: In the Côte de Beaune, south of Beaune, Chardonnay makes some of the world's greatest whites. Meursault is rich, nutty and buttery; Puligny-Montrachet elegant and floral; Chassagne-Montrachet fuller. Grand Crus like Le Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne are fermented and aged in oak, with great ageing potential.

steps.prompt: What is special about Chablis' Kimmeridgian soil?
steps.explanation: Kimmeridgian limestone and clay are full of fossilised oyster shells.

steps.title: Comparing them
steps.body: Chablis is cooler, leaner and more mineral, usually less oak. The Côte de Beaune is warmer, with riper fruit, more body and oak. Further south, the Mâconnais, with Pouilly-Fuissé, gives rounder, fruitier, good-value wines. All are 100% Chardonnay.
steps.highlight: Chablis lean; Côte de Beaune rich

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its style.
steps.explanation: Burgundy shows every side of Chardonnay.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chablis is lean and mineral on Kimmeridgian soil
The Côte de Beaune makes rich, oaked whites
The Mâconnais gives rounder, good-value wines
